sentence: Peripheral arterial disease, often called PAD, is a long-term condition that affects the blood supply to the legs and causes pain in the legs.
It is usually caused by arteries becoming narrowed or blocked, most often by fatty deposits building up in the artery walls, which is called atherosclerosis.
The most typical sign is calf pain on walking that settles with rest, although some people have no symptoms.
There is no cure, but lifestyle changes and medicine can help reduce the symptoms.
note: NHS: no cure for PAD, lifestyle changes and medicine can help reduce symptoms.

sentence: The NHS describes peripheral arterial disease, often shortened to PAD, as a long-term condition that affects the blood supply to the legs and causes pain in the legs.
The most typical sign is calf pain on walking that settles with rest, which is called intermittent claudication.
The pain can range from mild to severe and usually goes away after a few minutes of resting the legs.
The British Heart Foundation describes it as a cramp-like pain in the leg muscles that most commonly affects the calves.
Other possible signs include hair loss on the legs, shiny skin, numbness or weakness, slow-growing toenails and sores that do not heal.
A very weak or undetectable pulse in the leg can also be found.
Symptoms often start gradually, and some people with PAD have no symptoms at all.
note: NHS: some people have no symptoms; BHF: gradual start, many have none.

sentence: If the narrowing becomes severe, pain can come on at rest or wake a person at night, which is called critical limb ischaemia.
PAD is usually caused by the arteries that supply blood to the legs becoming narrowed or blocked.
The main cause is atherosclerosis, where fatty deposits build up in the artery walls.
The British Heart Foundation describes this as fatty material building up inside the arteries, which limits blood flow, mainly to the legs.
Less common causes include inflammatory blood vessel conditions such as vasculitis, and an injured or diseased artery.
Smoking is described as the most significant risk factor for PAD.
Diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and older age also raise the risk.
The same build-up can affect arteries elsewhere in the body, so PAD is linked to coronary heart disease, heart attack and stroke.
note: BHF: risk of coronary heart disease and stroke; NHLBI summary: plaque in other arteries including heart and brain.

sentence: A GP usually starts by examining the legs.
The GP may use a test called the ankle brachial pressure index, or ABPI, which compares blood pressure at the ankle with blood pressure in the arm.
Local NHS information says the test may be done at the GP surgery, or a person may be referred to a podiatry service.

sentence: A Cornwall NHS primary care guideline warns that a normal result does not always rule out PAD in people who have symptoms, particularly people with diabetes.

sentence: The NICE guideline on PAD covers assessing for the condition, imaging before treatment to restore blood flow, managing claudication and managing critical limb ischaemia.
NICE recommends duplex ultrasound as the first imaging test when treatment to restore blood flow is being considered.
Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiography is offered when more detail is needed before an intervention.
There is no cure for PAD, but lifestyle changes and medicine can help reduce the symptoms.

The British Heart Foundation says the first step is reducing the risk of heart attack and stroke, for example by stopping smoking, testing for and treating high blood pressure and diabetes, and taking a blood thinner such as aspirin and a statin.
The NHS describes walking as one of the best exercises, using a stop-start approach of walking until the pain builds, resting until it goes, then walking again.
note: Search summary of NHS treatment page.

sentence: NICE recommends that a supervised exercise programme is offered to people with intermittent claudication.
The British Heart Foundation notes that supervised walking programmes are not widely available on the NHS.
Surgery is generally considered when lifestyle changes and medicines are not enough.
Angioplasty is less invasive than bypass surgery and is generally preferred unless it is unsuitable or has failed before.
Bypass grafts use an artificial hollow tube or a vein taken from the leg or arm, and it is a larger operation.

The NICE quality standard says angioplasty for claudication is offered only when imaging has confirmed it is appropriate, advice on changing risk factors has been given and a supervised exercise programme has not improved symptoms.
The NHS says that if symptoms develop quickly or get suddenly worse, it could be a sign of a serious problem needing immediate treatment.
The British Heart Foundation explains that when blood supply worsens rapidly, rapid treatment is essential to have a chance of saving the leg.
In that situation the route to care is 999 or A&E, while symptoms that come on slowly are usually raised at a GP appointment.
note: The GP route is from NHS (see a GP for symptoms); the 999/A&E route is standard signposting not stated in the returned text.

sentence: Both angioplasty and bypass surgery carry a small risk of serious complications, such as heart attack, stroke and death.
The British Heart Foundation says there is no cure, but many people find that their PAD stays stable and their symptoms do not get worse.
How the condition progresses varies from person to person.
Because PAD is linked to coronary heart disease and stroke, treatment also aims to lower the risk of these.
